entry.title: LLDB Survival Guide: Theory, Tricks, and Python Hooks

link.title: LLDB Survival Guide: Theory, Tricks, and Python Hooks

entry.content:
LLDB is more than a place to set breakpoints. You can inspect app state, test quick fixes without rebuilding, and automate common debug steps. This guide keeps things practical and beginner-friendly.

Debugging with LLDB and Python hooks

Start Here: What LLDB Is and How to Run It

LLDB (sometimes typed as lldb in lowercase by mistake) is the debugger that ships with Xcode command line tools.

If your app is not running yet, launch it under LLDB:

xcrun lldb /path/to/MyApp

Then in the LLDB prompt:

(lldb) run

If your app is already running, attach to it:

pgrep -x MyApp
xcrun lldb -p <pid>

Or from inside LLDB:

(lldb) attach --name MyApp

To exit:

(lldb) quit

Why Attaching To Production Apps Can Fail

Many people hit this early: attaching to production macOS apps is often blocked by security rules.

Main reasons:

  • SIP (System Integrity Protection) blocks debugging many protected/system processes.
  • Hardened Runtime + missing get-task-allow entitlement can block debugger attach.
  • App Store/release builds are usually signed to prevent casual attaching.

So yes, sometimes attach starts working only after SIP is disabled on a test machine. But SIP is not the only gate. Even with SIP disabled, code-signing and entitlements can still block attach.

Check SIP status:

csrutil status

If you are doing local security research on your own Mac only, disable SIP temporarily:

  1. Reboot into Recovery.
  2. Open Terminal in Recovery.
  3. Run csrutil disable.
  4. Reboot normally.

Warning: this is dangerous. Disabling SIP removes important macOS protections that block system tampering and many privilege-escalation paths. If malware runs while SIP is off, it has a much easier time persisting and modifying protected files/processes. Do this only on an isolated test machine, never on your daily-use Mac, and re-enable SIP immediately after testing.

Re-enable it when done:

  1. Reboot into Recovery again.
  2. Run csrutil enable.
  3. Reboot normally.

A Fast Theory Primer

LLDB has two parts:

  • The command line you type into.
  • An internal toolkit called the SB API (SB = Script Bridge in LLDB docs).

Note: this is LLDB’s API naming and is different from the separate macOS ScriptingBridge framework.

What is the SB API object model?

It is just LLDB’s internal set of objects (like building blocks): app, process, thread, stack frame, variables, and symbols. LLDB commands use these objects behind the scenes.

Typical flow:

  • Create or select the app to debug (called a “target”): target create ...
  • Launch or attach: run / attach ...
  • Check liveness: process status
  • Inspect call stack and local values: frame info, frame variable -L (or alias v -L)

expr -- <code> runs code inside the paused app. Start with read-only checks. Only change values on purpose.

Quick Commands I Actually Use

(lldb) breakpoint set --name viewDidLoad
(lldb) thread step-in
(lldb) thread backtrace
(lldb) frame variable request
(lldb) expr -l objc -O -- [[[UIApplication sharedApplication] connectedScenes] allObjects]
(lldb) memory read --format x --size 8 --count 8 $sp

Speed tips: br s -n, bt, v (or frame var), and mem r are short versions of common commands. Use --one-shot true for temporary breakpoints so they remove themselves after one hit.

Anatomy of a Stop

LLDB can stop because of a breakpoint, crash signal, exception, or watchpoint. First step: find out why it stopped.

Common crash signals/exceptions you will see:

  • EXC_BAD_ACCESS / SIGSEGV: invalid memory access (use-after-free, null/garbage pointer).
  • SIGABRT: app called abort() (failed assertion, fatal error, uncaught runtime issue).
  • SIGILL: illegal CPU instruction (corrupted state, bad jump, unsupported instruction path).

process status tells you if you hit EXC_BAD_ACCESS, SIGSEGV, or a normal breakpoint. thread backtrace all shows what every thread is doing, which helps with hangs. thread return can skip the current function, but use it carefully because it changes app behavior.

Breakpoint vs watchpoint (quick difference):

  • Breakpoint: stops when execution reaches a code location (file/line/function).
  • Watchpoint: stops when a specific value in memory is read/written/modified.

If you get expected signals like SIGPIPE, tune handling explicitly:

process handle SIGPIPE -n true -p true -s false

Breakpoints That Pull Their Weight

br s -f File.swift -l 42 sets a breakpoint at one exact line. br s -r "viewDidLoad" matches many functions by name pattern. Conditional breakpoints like br s -n foo -c 'count > 10' stop only when a rule is true.

Auto-commands are great for data capture:

  • Set breakpoint: br s -n willDisplayCell
  • Add actions: br command add <id>
  • Add commands like thread backtrace, frame variable model, then continue

Watchpoints stop when a value changes:

  • watchpoint set variable myVar
  • watchpoint set variable -w read_write myVar
  • watchpoint set expression -w modify -- &myVar

Tracepoints Without Pausing

When you want logs but do not want to pause:

br s -n foo -C 'expr -O -- foo' -G true

Add --ignore-count to skip the first N hits.

Reading Swift Nicely

Swift values can look cleaner with these settings:

  • settings set target.swift-demangle true
  • settings set target.max-children-count 256
  • settings set target.process.optimization-warnings true

Use expr -l swift -O -- for Swift objects (equivalent to po with explicit Swift context) and expr -l objc -O -- for Objective-C objects. In Release/optimized builds, some local variables may be unavailable; this is normal.

Production/Optimized Build Survival

settings set symbols.enable-external-lookup true can help LLDB find extra symbol info. If local values are optimized away, check raw CPU registers (register read) and memory (memory read) near $sp/$fp.

Noise control while stepping:

settings append target.process.thread.step-avoid-libraries UIKitCore

thread jump --by 1 can skip one source line. Use as a last resort.

If tracing is supported in your environment, this sequence is useful:

  • thread trace start
  • thread trace dump instructions

Memory Work: From Sanity Checks to Surgery

Stack sanity check:

memory read --format x --size 8 --count 4 $fp

Address-to-symbol mapping:

image lookup -a 0xADDR

Controlled mutation during experiments:

  • expr -- myValue = 0
  • memory write <addr> <bytes>

For memory allocation history, try memory history <address> when available. For memory-region details, use memory region <address> and vmmap (a macOS terminal tool).

Async/Await, Actors, and Queues

thread list gives a quick view of active threads and queue names. thread info -s gives extra stop details.

Useful concurrency breakpoints:

  • br s -n _swift_task_switch
  • br s -n swift_task_enqueue

To find where a task was launched, break in the task body and inspect bt for concurrency runtime frames around your app frames.

Crash and Hang Triage Playbook

For hangs:

  1. process interrupt
  2. thread backtrace all
  3. Check for waits like pthread_mutex_lock and dispatch_semaphore_wait

For crashes, start with the crashing thread: run process status, then frame info on that thread. If shared state looks suspicious, add watchpoints and rerun.

To keep a point-in-time artifact for offline analysis:

process save-core /tmp/foo.core

Remote and Core-File Debugging

Remote iOS debugging usually starts with:

  • platform select remote-ios
  • platform connect connect://<host>:<port>

Then add symbols locally (target symbols add ...) and verify loaded images with image list.

For core files:

  • target create --core crash.core
  • thread backtrace all
  • thread select <index> to inspect specific crashed paths

Symbols and dSYMs

Keep .dSYM files available. They help LLDB map memory addresses back to file names and line numbers. Configure search paths in .lldbinit (target.exec-search-paths, target.debug-file-search-paths).

Verification loop:

  • image list -b for UUID/slide info
  • dwarfdump --uuid to confirm matches
  • fallback symbolication with atos -o MyApp -arch arm64 -l <slide> <addr> if needed

Python: Hooking Your Own Commands

LLDB supports Python. You can add your own custom commands. If you are new, you can skip this section and come back later.

# save as ~/lldb_tools/retain_cycles.py
import lldb

def find_retain_cycles(debugger, command, exe_ctx, result, _):
    """Demo command: run a Swift helper method on an expression."""
    cmd = f"expr -l swift -O -- {command}.debugRetainCycles()"
    res = lldb.SBCommandReturnObject()
    debugger.GetCommandInterpreter().HandleCommand(cmd, res)

    if res.Succeeded():
        result.AppendMessage(res.GetOutput() or "")
    else:
        result.SetError(res.GetError() or "Expression failed")

def __lldb_init_module(debugger, _internal_dict):
    debugger.HandleCommand(
        "command script add -f retain_cycles.find_retain_cycles rcfind"
    )
    print("Registered: rcfind <expression>")

Wire it in .lldbinit:

command script import ~/lldb_tools/retain_cycles.py

Use it in-session:

(lldb) rcfind myController

A More Involved Hook: Auto-Dump on Crash Stops

# ~/lldb_tools/on_crash_dump.py
import datetime
import lldb

CRASH_REASONS = {
    lldb.eStopReasonException,
    lldb.eStopReasonSignal,
}

class CrashDumpHook:
    def __init__(self, target, _extra_args, _internal_dict):
        self.target = target

    def handle_stop(self, exe_ctx, stream):
        thread = exe_ctx.GetThread()
        if not thread.IsValid():
            return False

        reason = thread.GetStopReason()
        if reason not in CRASH_REASONS:
            return False

        ts = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
        path = f"/tmp/lldb-crash-{ts}.txt"

        res = lldb.SBCommandReturnObject()
        interp = self.target.GetDebugger().GetCommandInterpreter()
        interp.HandleCommand("thread backtrace all", res)

        with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(f"Stop reason enum: {reason}\n\n")
            f.write(res.GetOutput() or "")

        stream.Printf(f"Wrote crash dump to {path}\n")
        return False

def __lldb_init_module(debugger, _dict):
    debugger.HandleCommand(
        "target stop-hook add -P on_crash_dump.CrashDumpHook"
    )
    print("Registered crash stop hook")

Add to .lldbinit:

command script import ~/lldb_tools/on_crash_dump.py

This saves crash dumps only on real crash-like stops, not on every breakpoint.

Favorite .lldbinit Snippets

settings set stop-disassembly-count 4
settings set target.process.thread.step-out-avoids-no-debug true
settings set target.process.thread.step-in-avoids-no-debug true
settings set target.max-children-count 256
settings set target.swift-demangle true
command alias bt thread backtrace
command alias frv frame variable -L
command alias memr memory read --format x --size 8 --count 8

Automating Sessions

Small automations that save time:

  • Keep recurring breakpoints in a file and load with command source my_breakpoints.lldb
  • Add quick diagnostics: target stop-hook add -o "thread backtrace"
  • Turn on protocol logging when needed: log enable gdb-remote packets

Performance Poking Without Instruments

For instruction-level hotspots:

  • thread step-inst
  • thread until -a <addr>

For symbol-focused checks:

  • image lookup -n objc_msgSend
  • br s -a <addr> with a suitable condition

statistics dump helps you see if LLDB itself is slow (for example, symbol loading or heavy expression use).

UI Debugging Without Xcode

Rendering and layout:

  • br s -n drawRect:
  • br s -n layoutSubviews

Responder-chain probing:

expr -l objc -O -- [UIResponder targetForAction:@selector(description) withSender:nil]

Text view hierarchy dump (old but still useful in UIKit debugging):

expr -l objc -O -- [[[UIApplication sharedApplication] keyWindow] recursiveDescription]

When LLDB Misbehaves

If LLDB starts slowly or acts weird, first simplify your .lldbinit. If module caches are broken, clear ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ModuleCache*.

If expressions fail unexpectedly, force the language:

  • expr -l objc -- ...
  • expr -l swift -- ...

If remote attach fails repeatedly, restart the target device and clean up stale debugserver processes on host and device.

Tiny Cheat Sheet (copy/paste)

br s -n method
br s -f File.swift -l 88
br s -n foo -c 'x > 3'
br s -n foo --one-shot true
watchpoint set variable -w read_write myVar
thread backtrace all
frame variable -L
expr -l swift -O -- myObj.debugDescription()
memory read --format x --size 8 --count 4 $sp
process handle SIGPIPE -n true -p true -s false

LLDB gets easier with repetition. Keep a small command list you trust, and add automation later.

entry.title: Phantom Types in Swift
entry.content:
Phantom types let you tuck extra meaning into Swift’s type system without changing anything at runtime. A phantom type is a generic parameter that is never stored. It exists only so the compiler can tell apart values that look identical in memory: meters and feet, a user ID and an order ID, an email address you’ve validated and one you haven’t. If you are new to Swift’s type system, think of phantom types as labels the compiler reads, not values your app carries around.

Phantom Types in Swift: identical values, distinct type tags

The basic idea

Consider a Tagged wrapper that carries a Raw value and a phantom Tag type:

struct Tagged<Tag, Raw> {
    var raw: Raw
    init(_ raw: Raw) { self.raw = raw }
}

Tag is never used in a stored property, but it is still part of the type. Tagged<A, Double> and Tagged<B, Double> are as different to the compiler as Int and String, even though both are just a Double in memory.

Tags are usually empty enums:

enum MetersTag {}
enum FeetTag {}

An enum with no cases can’t be instantiated, which is exactly what you want: nobody should ever create a “value” of MetersTag. It only exists to be a name the compiler can check.

Because the tag isn’t stored, the wrapper is the same size as the raw value:

MemoryLayout<Tagged<MetersTag, Double>>.size // 8, same as Double

Eliminating category errors

In 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one piece of software produced thrust data in pound-force seconds while another expected newton-seconds. Both were just numbers. Phantom types make this kind of mix-up a compile error:

typealias Meters = Tagged<MetersTag, Double>
typealias Feet   = Tagged<FeetTag, Double>

func climb(by height: Meters) { /* ... */ }

let ladder = Feet(12)
climb(by: ladder) // ❌ cannot convert value of type 'Feet' to expected argument type 'Meters'

A wrapper that can’t do arithmetic gets annoying fast, so give it the operations that make sense. Notice that + takes two values of the same Self, so adding meters to feet still doesn’t compile:

extension Tagged: Equatable where Raw: Equatable {}

extension Tagged: AdditiveArithmetic where Raw: AdditiveArithmetic {
    static var zero: Self { Self(.zero) }
    static func + (lhs: Self, rhs: Self) -> Self { Self(lhs.raw + rhs.raw) }
    static func - (lhs: Self, rhs: Self) -> Self { Self(lhs.raw - rhs.raw) }
}

extension Tagged where Raw: Numeric {
    static func * (lhs: Self, rhs: Raw) -> Self { Self(lhs.raw * rhs) }
}

let total = Meters(3) + Meters(4)   // ✅ Meters(7)
let double = total * 2              // ✅ Meters(14)
// Meters(3) + Feet(4)              // ❌ won't compile

Tags that carry information

Tags can’t hold instance data, but they can conform to protocols and provide static data. That lets the tag itself know how to convert. This version replaces the MetersTag/FeetTag design above, so Meters and Feet are now the tags themselves:

protocol LengthUnit {
    static var metersPerUnit: Double { get }
}

enum Meters: LengthUnit { static let metersPerUnit = 1.0 }
enum Feet: LengthUnit { static let metersPerUnit = 0.3048 }

typealias Length<Unit: LengthUnit> = Tagged<Unit, Double>

extension Tagged where Tag: LengthUnit, Raw == Double {
    func converted<Target: LengthUnit>(to _: Target.Type) -> Length<Target> {
        Length<Target>(raw * Tag.metersPerUnit / Target.metersPerUnit)
    }
}

let run = Length<Meters>(5_000)
let runInFeet = run.converted(to: Feet.self) // ≈ 16,404.2 ft

Conversions are now explicit and correct by construction. You can’t forget one, because the types won’t line up, and you can’t apply the wrong factor, because the factor comes from the tag.

Foundation’s Measurement<UnitType> uses a related idea. Its generic parameter (UnitLength, UnitMass, …) stops you from adding a length to a mass, while the specific unit (meters or feet) is stored at runtime and converted for you. If you need units that the user picks at runtime, Measurement is often the better tool. Phantom tags fit best when the unit is fixed in code.

Identifiers that can’t be swapped

Every model has an ID, and they’re often all UUID or String. A popular trick is to use the model type itself as the tag:

struct User {
    typealias ID = Tagged<User, UUID>
    let id: ID
}

struct Order {
    typealias ID = Tagged<Order, UUID>
    let id: ID
    let userID: User.ID
}

func cancel(_ order: Order.ID) { /* ... */ }

cancel(order.id)     // ✅
cancel(order.userID) // ❌ cannot convert value of type 'User.ID' to expected argument type 'Order.ID'

There’s no circular-type problem here: Tagged never stores a User, so User can mention its own type in its ID.

Phantom types as proof of a check

This is where phantom types become really useful, and also where it’s easiest to get them wrong.

A tag like Verified is a claim. The compiler checks that only Email<Verified> values reach sendWelcome(to:), but it doesn’t know what “verified” means. The guarantee is only as strong as the rule for who is allowed to create a verified value. If anyone can write Email<Verified>("whatever"), the tag is worthless.

So the key is access control: make the general initializer private to one file, and expose only the paths that actually perform the check.

enum Unverified {}
enum Verified {}

struct Email<Status> {
    let address: String

    // Only code in this file can create an email with an arbitrary status.
    fileprivate init(address: String) { self.address = address }
}

extension Email where Status == Unverified {
    init(_ address: String) { self.init(address: address) }

    func verified() -> Email<Verified>? {
        guard address.contains("@") else { return nil } // stand-in for real validation
        return Email<Verified>(address: address)
    }
}

func sendWelcome(to email: Email<Verified>) { /* ... */ }

From any other file:

let input = Email<Unverified>("sam@example.com")

sendWelcome(to: input)                        // ❌ Unverified isn't Verified
let forged = Email<Verified>(address: "x")    // ❌ the general initializer is fileprivate
if let email = input.verified() {
    sendWelcome(to: email)                    // ✅
}

Once the value exists, functions downstream never need to re-validate it. The type is the proof that validation happened. This pattern is often summed up as “parse, don’t validate.”

A note on SQL

SQL is a common phantom-types example, usually with a sanitize() function that turns Raw SQL into Safe SQL. Be careful with that idea: escaping user input into a query string is fragile and is not how you prevent SQL injection. The reliable fix is parameterized queries, where user values are bound separately from the SQL text and never become part of it.

A phantom type can still help, by guaranteeing that the SQL text came from your source code and not from user input. StaticString only accepts string literals, so it’s a neat way to enforce that:

enum Trusted {}

struct Query<Trust> {
    let sql: String
    fileprivate init(sql: String) { self.sql = sql }
}

extension Query where Trust == Trusted {
    init(_ sql: StaticString) { self.init(sql: sql.description) }
}

func execute(_ query: Query<Trusted>, parameters: [any Sendable] = []) { /* bind and run */ }

execute(Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"), parameters: [userID]) // ✅

let name = readLine()!
execute(Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '\(name)'")) // ❌ an interpolated string is not a StaticString

The type system now forces every caller to pass user data as parameters.

Coordinate spaces

The same trick keeps coordinate systems honest:

enum ViewSpace {}
enum WorldSpace {}

struct Point<Space> {
    var x: Double
    var y: Double
}

typealias ViewPoint  = Point<ViewSpace>
typealias WorldPoint = Point<WorldSpace>

func toWorld(_ p: ViewPoint, scale: Double, origin: WorldPoint) -> WorldPoint {
    WorldPoint(x: origin.x + p.x / scale, y: origin.y + p.y / scale)
}

// Works in any space, but both points must be in the *same* one.
func distance<Space>(_ a: Point<Space>, _ b: Point<Space>) -> Double {
    ((a.x - b.x) * (a.x - b.x) + (a.y - b.y) * (a.y - b.y)).squareRoot()
}

let tap = ViewPoint(x: 10, y: 20)
let world = toWorld(tap, scale: 2, origin: WorldPoint(x: 0, y: 0))
// toWorld(world, ...)  // ❌ can't convert a point that's already in world space
// distance(tap, world) // ❌ conflicting arguments to generic parameter 'Space'

The distance function shows a nice property: generic code can work with any tag while still requiring that tags match.

State machines (typestate)

You can also tag a value with the step it’s in, so only valid transitions exist. This is called the typestate pattern:

enum Welcome {}
enum Permissions {}
enum Completed {}

struct Answers { var allowsNotifications = false }

struct Onboarding<Step>: ~Copyable {
    fileprivate var answers: Answers
    fileprivate init(answers: Answers) { self.answers = answers }
}

extension Onboarding where Step == Welcome {
    init() { self.init(answers: Answers()) }

    consuming func next() -> Onboarding<Permissions> {
        Onboarding<Permissions>(answers: answers)
    }
}

extension Onboarding where Step == Permissions {
    consuming func finish(allowingNotifications allowed: Bool) -> Onboarding<Completed> {
        var answers = answers
        answers.allowsNotifications = allowed
        return Onboarding<Completed>(answers: answers)
    }
}

Two details make this actually safe, and both are easy to leave out:

  1. The initializer is fileprivate. Otherwise anyone could create an Onboarding<Completed> directly and skip the steps entirely.
  2. The type is ~Copyable and the transitions are consuming. Without this, nothing stops you from reusing an old state after moving on:
func startOnboarding() {
    let welcome = Onboarding<Welcome>()
    let permissions = welcome.next()
    let again = welcome.next() // ❌ 'welcome' consumed more than once
}

(This needs to live inside a function: Swift doesn’t allow consuming a noncopyable global variable.)

Transitions are methods in constrained extensions (where Step == Permissions), so finish simply doesn’t exist on a Welcome value, and autocomplete only offers the valid next step. Noncopyable types need Swift 5.9 or later; on older toolchains you still get the step checking but not the “no reuse” guarantee.

More places phantom types help

  • Auth state. A Session<Authenticated> can only come from a login function that actually checked credentials, and APIs that need a logged-in user take that type. Login status is decided at runtime, so the tag doesn’t replace the check. It records that the check happened, the same way Email<Verified> does.
  • Versioned payloads. Tag decoded data as Payload<V1> or Payload<V2>, and make migration functions the only way to go from one to the other.
  • Bytes and encodings. Tag buffers as BigEndian/LittleEndian, or plaintext versus encrypted Data, so a raw buffer can’t be sent where an encrypted one is expected.
  • Color spaces. Tag colors as SRGB or DisplayP3 and make conversion an explicit function.

Not everything is a good fit. A runtime feature flag, for example, can’t be a phantom type on its own: the compiler can’t know at build time whether the flag is on. Phantom types describe facts the code can establish statically, or facts a specific function has checked.

Designing phantom types well

Keep tag types empty and name them for intent (Verified, Meters, WorldSpace) so the purpose is clear at the call site. Use typealiases to keep signatures readable.

Put protocol conformances on the wrapper, conditionally on Raw, so tagged values behave like the values they wrap:

extension Tagged: Hashable where Raw: Hashable {}
extension Tagged: Sendable where Raw: Sendable {}

extension Tagged: Comparable where Raw: Comparable {
    static func < (lhs: Self, rhs: Self) -> Bool { lhs.raw < rhs.raw }
}

extension Tagged: CustomStringConvertible {
    var description: String { String(describing: raw) }
}

Note that description only takes effect in print and string interpolation when you declare the CustomStringConvertible conformance. A plain var description in an extension is just an ordinary property.

Encode as the raw value. If you let Swift synthesize Codable, a tagged ID is encoded as an object, {"raw": "E621E1F8-..."}, which almost certainly isn’t what your API sends. Encode through a single-value container instead:

extension Tagged: Codable where Raw: Codable {
    init(from decoder: Decoder) throws {
        self.init(try decoder.singleValueContainer().decode(Raw.self))
    }

    func encode(to encoder: Encoder) throws {
        var container = encoder.singleValueContainer()
        try container.encode(raw)
    }
}

Now User can stay Codable and its id decodes straight from "id": "E621E1F8-..." in JSON, which also takes care of “tag on entry”: the value is tagged the moment it’s decoded.

Be aware that conditional conformances apply to every tag. If Tagged is Comparable, so is User.ID, even if ordering IDs is meaningless. That’s usually harmless, but for wrappers that represent proof (like Email<Verified>), prefer a dedicated struct with exactly the API you want.

If you don’t want to write all of this yourself, Point-Free’s open-source swift-tagged library provides a Tagged type with these conformances and more.

Pitfalls to avoid

A public initializer defeats the purpose. If the tag means “this has been checked”, restrict who can create tagged values, as shown in the Email and Onboarding examples. Unit and ID tags don’t need this, because there’s nothing to check.

A typealias is not a new type. typealias UserID = UUID gives you no safety at all; UserID and UUID are interchangeable. The same goes for two aliases of the same tagged type: typealias AdminID = Tagged<User, UUID> is exactly User.ID. The safety comes from the tag, so each concept needs its own tag type.

The tag must be known at compile time. If the kind of value is only decided at runtime (a user choosing a unit, a server sending either version), you can’t pick a phantom type dynamically. Use an enum or Measurement, then convert to the right tagged type once you know which case you have.

Don’t tag everything. Overuse makes APIs noisy and error messages long. Save phantom types for places where mixing values would be a real bug.

Tag on entry, untag on exit. Wrap raw values at the boundary (decoding, database reads, user input) so untagged values never flow into your core logic, and only unwrap raw where you hand data to the outside world.

Testing phantom-heavy code

Most of the guarantees are enforced by the compiler, so your runtime tests should focus on what the compiler can’t check: the validation logic, the conversion factors, and the encoding shape. With Swift Testing:

import Testing
import Foundation
@testable import MyApp

@Test func rejectsInvalidEmail() {
    #expect(Email<Unverified>("not-an-email").verified() == nil)
}

@Test func convertsMetersToFeet() {
    let feet = Length<Meters>(1).converted(to: Feet.self)
    #expect(abs(feet.raw - 3.28084) < 0.0001)
}

@Test func idsEncodeAsPlainValues() throws {
    let id = User.ID(UUID(uuidString: "E621E1F8-C36C-495A-93FC-0C247A3E6E5F")!)
    let json = String(decoding: try JSONEncoder().encode(id), as: UTF8.self)
    #expect(json == #""E621E1F8-C36C-495A-93FC-0C247A3E6E5F""#)
}

What about checking that bad code doesn’t compile? Neither XCTest nor Swift Testing can do that: a test file that fails to compile breaks the whole test target. If a guarantee is critical (for example, that Email<Verified> can’t be forged), keep a small “must not compile” file outside your targets and type-check it in CI:

# Fails the build if forged_email.swift compiles.
if swiftc -typecheck Sources/MyApp/Email.swift NegativeTests/forged_email.swift 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "error: NegativeTests/forged_email.swift should not compile"
  exit 1
fi

This only works when the files you pass to swiftc are self-contained, so keep the types you check this way in small files with few dependencies. Also note that -typecheck stops before the compiler’s ownership checks, so it won’t catch “consumed more than once” errors from the typestate example. For those, use swiftc -emit-sil -wmo instead, which runs the full checks without producing a binary.

Performance

The tag costs nothing at runtime: it has no storage, and MemoryLayout confirms the wrapper is the same size as the raw value. The wrapper’s methods are tiny and normally get inlined.

The one thing to know is that generic code isn’t always specialized. Within a module, or with whole-module optimization, the compiler usually specializes and inlines everything. Across module boundaries, a generic function the compiler can’t see into may run through slower unspecialized code. If you ship Tagged in a library and use it in hot loops, mark the small helpers @inlinable, and measure before you worry about it.

When to reach for phantom types

Reach for phantom types when you want the compiler to stop domain mix-ups: units (meters versus feet), identifiers (user versus order), coordinate spaces (view versus world), steps in a flow, or trust levels (unverified versus verified). They shine when a runtime check would be easy to forget, and when many concepts share the same behavior, so one generic wrapper replaces a dozen near-identical structs.

Consider the alternatives too:

  • A dedicated struct (struct UserID { let raw: UUID }) is simpler and clearer when you have only one or two such types.
  • An enum fits when the variant is chosen at runtime.
  • Measurement is the standard answer for physical units that need runtime conversion and formatting.

Phantom types are a gentle way to make invalid states unrepresentable in Swift. They turn assumptions into rules the compiler enforces. Start with one hotspot (IDs, units, a validated input), tag it at the boundary, push the tag through your pipeline, and only expand when the safety win is clear.

Further reading

  • swift-tagged: a production-ready Tagged type from Point-Free.
  • SE-0390: Noncopyable structs and enums: the feature behind the typestate example.
  • Parse, don’t validate by Alexis King: the idea behind “phantom types as proof of a check.”
entry.summary: Phantom types let you tuck extra meaning into Swift’s type system without changing anything at runtime. A phantom type is a generic parameter that is never stored. It exists only so the compiler can tell apart values that look identical in memory: meters and feet, a user ID and an order ID, an email address you’ve validated and one you haven’t. If you are new to Swift’s type system, think of phantom types as labels the compiler reads, not values your app carries around.

entry.title: Setting Up a New macOS Device: My Essential Tweaks

link.title: Setting Up a New macOS Device: My Essential Tweaks

entry.content:
Getting a new Mac is always exciting, but the first few hours are usually spent setting things up just the way you like them. Here’s a collection of my favorite customizations, terminal tweaks, and productivity hacks that I always apply on a fresh macOS installation.

Personalizing a new macOS developer setup

A quick note before we start: many tweaks below use defaults write, which edits the preference files apps read on launch. They’re safe and reversible. To undo any of them, run the same command with defaults delete and the same domain and key (for example defaults delete com.apple.dock autohide-delay), then restart the affected app. To see a setting’s current value, use defaults read with the same domain and key.

First Things First: Developer Tools

Install Apple’s command line tools (Git, clang, make, and friends). You can skip this if you’re installing the full Xcode, which includes them:

xcode-select --install

Then install Homebrew, the package manager most Mac developers use. Copy the install command from the Homebrew website rather than from a blog post, so you always get the current version. On Apple silicon Macs, Homebrew installs into /opt/homebrew, and the installer prints two commands at the end to add it to your PATH. Run them, or brew won’t be found in new terminal windows.

💡 Tip: Homebrew can save and restore your whole setup. On your old Mac:

brew bundle dump --file=~/Brewfile

This writes every formula, cask (GUI app), and Mac App Store app you have installed into a Brewfile. On the new Mac, copy the file over and run:

brew bundle --file=~/Brewfile

Keep the Brewfile in a Git repository with your dotfiles, and setting up the next Mac becomes a single command.

Personalizing the Dock

The Dock is where your most-used apps live, but sometimes you want to create a little breathing room between groups of apps. That’s where empty spacer tiles come in.

To add one:

defaults write com.apple.dock persistent-apps -array-add '{"tile-type"="spacer-tile";}'; killall Dock

The macOS Dock with spacer tiles

Each time you run the command, it adds a blank space at the end of the apps section of your Dock. Drag the spacers to where you want them, just like app icons.

  • Use small-spacer-tile instead of spacer-tile for a half-width gap.
  • Use persistent-others instead of persistent-apps to add a spacer to the right side of the Dock, next to the Downloads folder and the Trash.
  • To remove a spacer, drag it out of the Dock until “Remove” appears, then let go.

If you hide the Dock, you can also get rid of the short delay before it slides in:

defaults write com.apple.dock autohide-delay -float 0; killall Dock

Preventing Sleep During Long Tasks

Sometimes you need your Mac awake for hours, like when running long builds, downloads, or data migrations. The simplest approach:

caffeinate -dis
  • caffeinate uses a single dash (-) followed by one or more flags.
  • The flags can be combined, so -dis is equivalent to -d -i -s.

Here’s what each flag does:

  • -d → Prevent the display from sleeping
  • -i → Prevent the system from idle sleeping
  • -s → Prevent the system from sleeping at all, even if you close the lid, but only while plugged into power
  • -u → Declare that the user is active, which turns the display on if it’s off

You’ll often see caffeinate -disu recommended, but -u doesn’t add much here. Without a timeout, its assertion only lasts 5 seconds, so it just wakes the display once. -d is what keeps the display on.

⚡ caffeinate --disu won’t work. caffeinate doesn’t support GNU-style double-dash options and fails with illegal option -- -.

As long as the caffeinate process runs, your Mac stays awake. Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

💡 Tip: Instead of running it forever, you can tie caffeinate to something with a natural end:

caffeinate -i xcodebuild        # stay awake while this command runs
caffeinate -i -t 3600           # stay awake for one hour (in seconds)
caffeinate -i -w 12345          # stay awake until process 12345 exits

When the command finishes, the timer runs out, or the process exits, your Mac goes back to its normal sleep behavior. The -w form is handy when you’ve already started a long job and forgot to wrap it: find its process ID with pgrep or Activity Monitor.

You can see what’s currently keeping your Mac awake with:

pmset -g assertions

Terminal Tweaks

Out of the box, macOS Terminal is functional, but a little bland. A few tweaks make it a more comfortable workspace.

Check your shell:

echo $SHELL

Since macOS Catalina, new user accounts default to Zsh (/bin/zsh). $SHELL shows your login shell, so if you’ve switched to a different one, this tells you what new terminal windows will start with. To customize your prompt, add this to ~/.zshrc:

PROMPT="%n %1~ %# "
  • %n → your username
  • %1~ → the current directory, with your home folder shown as ~
  • %# → % for a normal user, # when running as root

PROMPT and PS1 are the same variable in Zsh, so you’ll see both in examples online.

Reload with:

source ~/.zshrc

Pair it with a nice terminal theme (Solarized, Dracula, or Catppuccin are great choices), and you’ll have a much more pleasant developer experience.

💡 Extra ideas:

  • Install iTerm2 for split panes, better search, and more shortcuts.
  • Add zsh-autosuggestions and zsh-syntax-highlighting for a smoother typing flow. Installing them with brew install isn’t enough on its own: Homebrew prints a source ... line for each one, which you need to add to your ~/.zshrc. Keep zsh-syntax-highlighting as the last line sourced, as its README recommends.

Use Touch ID for sudo

Typing your password for every sudo gets old quickly. Since macOS Sonoma, you can enable Touch ID in a file that survives system updates:

sed "s/^#auth/auth/" /etc/pam.d/sudo_local.template | sudo tee /etc/pam.d/sudo_local

This copies Apple’s template and uncomments its single pam_tid.so line. Open a new terminal window, and sudo will ask for your fingerprint. (On older versions of macOS, people edited /etc/pam.d/sudo directly, but updates overwrite that file.) This doesn’t work over SSH or inside tmux without an extra helper, and falls back to your password in those cases.

Making Typing Snappier

If you type fast, macOS’s default key repeat rates feel sluggish. System Settings → Keyboard has sliders for both, but they stop at fairly conservative values. You can go further from the terminal:

defaults write -g InitialKeyRepeat -int 15
defaults write -g KeyRepeat -int 2
  • InitialKeyRepeat is how long you hold a key before it starts repeating.
  • KeyRepeat is the interval between repeated characters.

Both are measured in units of about 15 milliseconds, so lower numbers are faster. 15 and 2 are the fastest values the System Settings sliders allow, and they’re a good place to start. Many people go lower (10 and 1 are popular), but at those values it becomes easy to type a character twice by accident, including in your password on the login screen. Go down gradually and stop when it feels right.

Log out and back in for the changes to take effect.

And if you hate the popup menu that appears when holding a key, instead of just repeating it, disable it:

defaults write -g ApplePressAndHoldEnabled -bool false

Quit and reopen apps for this to take effect.

💡 Tip: If you regularly type in multiple languages, you may prefer keeping the popup enabled, since it helps you access accented characters quickly.

Finder Tweaks

Finder can be friendlier with a few quick adjustments. Start by enabling the status bar (bottom of Finder windows), so you can always see the number of items and available disk space:

  • View > Show Status Bar (⌘/)

I also recommend enabling the path bar, so you can see exactly where you are in the filesystem hierarchy. You can double-click any folder in it to jump there:

  • View > Show Path Bar (⌥⌘P)

A few more settings I always change:

# Always show file extensions
defaults write NSGlobalDomain AppleShowAllExtensions -bool true

# Search the current folder by default, instead of the whole Mac
defaults write com.apple.finder FXDefaultSearchScope -string "SCcf"

killall Finder

You can also set both of these in Finder > Settings > Advanced.

To toggle hidden files (like .gitignore or .zshrc) in any Finder window or Open dialog, press ⇧⌘. (Shift-Command-Period).

💡 Extra ideas:

  • Enable View > Show Tab Bar (⇧⌘T) to work with multiple Finder tabs like in a browser.
  • Use View > As Columns for a fast, hierarchical view when navigating deep folders.
  • Add common folders to the sidebar for one-click access, by dragging them in or pressing ⌃⌘T with a folder selected.

Switch between views with:

  • ⌘1 → Icon View
  • ⌘2 → List View
  • ⌘3 → Column View
  • ⌘4 → Gallery View

Note: In Column View, double-click the divider to the right of a column to resize it to fit its longest name. Hold Option while double-clicking to resize every column at once.

Auto-resizing a Finder column

Screenshots

By default, screenshots land on your Desktop, which quickly gets messy. Press ⇧⌘5, open Options, and pick another folder under Save to. Or do it from the terminal:

mkdir -p ~/Pictures/Screenshots
defaults write com.apple.screencapture location ~/Pictures/Screenshots

The folder must exist first, so don’t skip the mkdir.

Git Worktrees for Clean Development

When working with multiple Git branches, I prefer using worktrees instead of constantly switching branches back and forth. A worktree is an extra working directory attached to the same repository, so you can have two branches checked out side by side, each with its own files and build products.

Example:

git worktree add ../wt/app_name/feature_two feature_two

This creates a new directory with the existing branch feature_two checked out, perfect for parallel development without stashing or committing half-finished work in your main folder. The worktrees share one repository, so commits, branches, and fetches made in one are visible in all of them.

To create a new branch at the same time, add -b:

git worktree add -b feature_three ../wt/app_name/feature_three

💡 Extra ideas:

  • Use git worktree list to see all your active worktrees.
  • Use git worktree remove path/to/worktree to clean up old ones. Git refuses if the worktree has uncommitted changes, which protects you from losing work.
  • If you deleted a worktree folder by hand, run git worktree prune to clear Git’s leftover record of it.
  • Git won’t let you check out the same branch in two worktrees at once, so if worktree add fails, check whether that branch is already open somewhere else.
  • Keep worktrees in one place, like ~/Projects/wt/, so they’re easy to find and clean up.

Smarter Window Management with Rectangle

Since macOS Sequoia, macOS has built-in window tiling: drag a window to the edge of the screen, or use Window > Move & Resize and its shortcuts (like Fn-Control-arrow keys). If you want more layouts and fully customizable shortcuts, Rectangle is the go-to tool. It’s free and open source, and it lets you move and resize windows quickly from the keyboard.

💡 Why it’s great:

  • Snap windows to halves, thirds, quarters, or sixths of the screen.
  • Move windows between displays instantly.
  • Pick your own shortcuts for every action.

If you have a keyboard with a numeric keypad, you can bind Rectangle’s shortcuts to keypad keys so the keypad works like a map of your screen. Here’s one layout:

  • Keypad 7 / 8 / 9 → Top left, top center, top right
  • Keypad 4 / 5 / 6 → Left third, center third, right third
  • Keypad 1 / 2 / 3 → Bottom left, bottom center, bottom right

Or a simpler one built from halves and corners:

  • Keypad 8 → Top half
  • Keypad 2 → Bottom half
  • Keypad 4 → Left half
  • Keypad 6 → Right half
  • Keypad 7 / 9 / 1 / 3 → Corners (quarters)
  • Keypad 5 → Maximize

This way, you can manage windows with one hand, without dragging them around. Laptop keyboards don’t have a keypad, so on a MacBook stick with Rectangle’s default shortcuts (Control-Option plus arrow keys and letters).

Bonus: Small Things for Xcode Users

Show how long each build took, right in Xcode’s activity area:

defaults write com.apple.dt.Xcode ShowBuildOperationDuration -bool YES

Restart Xcode afterwards.

And if you work on iOS apps, xcrun simctl lets you manage simulators from the terminal: xcrun simctl list devices shows them all, and xcrun simctl delete unavailable removes simulators for runtimes you no longer have installed, which can free a surprising amount of disk space.

Wrapping Up

Most of this takes a few minutes, but it adds up to a Mac that feels like yours. The trick to never doing it by hand again: put the commands from this post in a shell script, keep it next to your Brewfile and dotfiles in a Git repository, and run it on every new machine.
entry.summary: Getting a new Mac is always exciting, but the first few hours are usually spent setting things up just the way you like them. Here’s a collection of my favorite customizations, terminal tweaks, and productivity hacks that I always apply on a fresh macOS installation.

entry.title: Clean Code in Swift
entry.content:
Clean code is code that the next person, often you in six months, can read, trust, and change without fear. Swift gives you unusually good tools for it: expressive naming conventions, value types, optionals, enums, and a compiler that catches whole classes of mistakes. Here are the habits that make the biggest difference in day-to-day Swift.

1. Names that read like sentences

Swift’s API Design Guidelines put clarity at the point of use first. Names should make call sites read naturally:

struct Inbox {
    private(set) var messages: [String] = []

    // ✅ Reads as a phrase at the call site: inbox.insert(message, at: 0)
    mutating func insert(_ message: String, at index: Int) {
        messages.insert(message, at: index)
    }

    // ✅ Boolean properties read as assertions
    var isEmpty: Bool { messages.isEmpty }
}

var inbox = Inbox()
inbox.insert("Welcome!", at: 0)

Avoid abbreviations (usr, mgr), type names in variable names (messagesArray), and vague words like data, info, handle, or process. For more, see Mastering Swift Style Guides.

2. Small functions that do one thing

If a function needs a comment to explain its sections, those sections probably want to be functions:

struct Order {
    var items: [Double]
    var couponPercent: Double
}

func total(for order: Order) -> Double {
    let subtotal = order.items.reduce(0, +)
    return applyDiscount(to: subtotal, percent: order.couponPercent)
}

private func applyDiscount(to amount: Double, percent: Double) -> Double {
    amount * (1 - percent / 100)
}

Each function has one reason to change, and its name tells you what it does without reading the body.

3. Flatten with guard

Deep nesting hides the main path. Check preconditions up front and exit early:

struct SignUpForm {
    var email: String?
    var password: String?
    var acceptedTerms: Bool
}

enum SignUpError: Error {
    case missingEmail, weakPassword, termsNotAccepted
}

func validate(_ form: SignUpForm) throws -> (email: String, password: String) {
    guard let email = form.email, !email.isEmpty else { throw SignUpError.missingEmail }
    guard let password = form.password, password.count >= 8 else { throw SignUpError.weakPassword }
    guard form.acceptedTerms else { throw SignUpError.termsNotAccepted }
    return (email, password)
}

4. Make invalid states unrepresentable

Booleans and optionals that must be kept in sync are a bug waiting to happen:

// ❌ Which combinations are valid? isLoading && error != nil?
struct ScreenStateFlags {
    var isLoading: Bool
    var items: [String]?
    var error: Error?
}

// ✅ Exactly one state at a time, each with its own data
enum ScreenState {
    case loading
    case loaded([String])
    case failed(Error)
}

The enum version can’t be in a contradictory state, and every switch over it must handle all cases. See Enumerations in Swift.

5. Prefer values and let

  • Use let by default; switch to var only when something really changes.
  • Prefer structs over classes, so data can’t change behind your back. See Structures and Classes.
  • Prefer non-mutating transformations, like map and filter, for data flow:
let prices = [12.0, 7.5, 30.0]
let affordable = prices.filter { $0 < 20 }.map { $0 * 1.2 }

6. Don’t force-unwrap your way out

Every ! is a promise that something is never nil. Sometimes that’s true, like a URL from a string literal you control, but usually it’s a crash waiting to happen. Use if let, guard let, ??, or a non-optional type instead:

let input = "42"
let quantity = Int(input) ?? 1          // ✅ explicit fallback
// let quantity = Int(input)!           // ❌ crashes on bad input

7. Depend on abstractions at the edges

Code that talks to the network, the database, or the clock is hard to test. Put a small protocol in front of it:

protocol Clock {
    var now: Date { get }
}

struct SystemClock: Clock {
    var now: Date { Date() }
}

struct SessionValidator {
    let clock: any Clock

    func isExpired(_ expiry: Date) -> Bool {
        clock.now > expiry
    }
}

Tests can pass a fixed clock, and the production code doesn’t change. Test Doubles in Swift shows this pattern in depth.

8. Handle errors honestly

  • Throw descriptive errors instead of returning nil when the caller needs to know why something failed.
  • Never silently swallow errors with an empty catch {}; at minimum, log them.
  • Reserve fatalError and precondition for programmer errors, not for user input or network failures.

9. Comments explain why

Code says what it does; comments should say what code can’t:

// Apple's API returns the cached value for up to 5 minutes after a change,
// so we bypass the cache right after the user edits their profile.
let shouldBypassCache = true

Delete commented-out code (that’s what version control is for), and keep // MARK: - sections to organize long files.

10. Let the tools help

  • Compiler warnings are free code review; aim for zero.
  • swift-format or SwiftLint keep formatting consistent, so code reviews can focus on design.
  • Swift 6 language mode catches data races at compile time.
  • Tests make refactoring safe, and refactoring is how code stays clean.

Summary

  • Name things for clarity at the call site, and keep functions small and focused.
  • Use guard for early exits, enums to rule out invalid states, and let and value types by default.
  • Avoid force-unwraps, put protocols in front of side effects, and handle errors explicitly.
  • Comment the why, and let the compiler, formatters, and tests keep the code honest.

Swift gives you unusually good tools for it: expressive naming conventions, value types, optionals, enums, and a compiler that catches whole classes of mistakes. Here are the habits that make the biggest difference in day-to-day Swift.

entry.title: Swift Evolution: How the Language Changes

link.title: Swift Evolution: How the Language Changes

entry.content:
Every Swift feature you use, from async/await to if expressions to macros, went through a public process before it shipped. That process is Swift Evolution. Anyone can read the proposals, follow the discussions, and take part. Knowing how it works helps you understand why Swift is designed the way it is, and what’s coming next.

Where it happens

  • The swift-evolution repository on GitHub (swiftlang/swift-evolution) holds every proposal, numbered SE-0001, SE-0002, and so on.
  • The Swift Forums (forums.swift.org) host the discussions: early ideas in Pitches, formal reviews in Proposal Reviews.
  • swift.org/swift-evolution offers a searchable dashboard of all proposals and their status.

The life of a proposal

  1. Pitch. Someone posts an idea on the forums. The community discusses whether the problem is real and the direction is right. Most ideas are refined, merged with others, or dropped here.
  2. Proposal. The idea is written up from the official template: motivation, proposed solution, detailed design, source and ABI compatibility, and alternatives considered.
  3. Implementation. A working implementation in the compiler or standard library is required before review, often available behind an experimental flag or in a toolchain snapshot.
  4. Review. The proposal is scheduled for a public review, usually about two weeks, managed by a review manager from the relevant workgroup. Anyone can post feedback.
  5. Decision. The Language Steering Group (or another workgroup, depending on the area) decides: accepted, accepted with modifications, returned for revision, or rejected.
  6. Release. Accepted proposals ship in a future Swift version. The proposal status shows which one, for example “Implemented (Swift 5.9)”.

Reading a proposal

A proposal’s sections are useful well beyond the decision:

  • Motivation explains the problem, often with the code people had to write before.
  • Detailed design is the precise specification, more exact than most documentation.
  • Source compatibility says whether existing code keeps compiling.
  • Alternatives considered explains rejected designs, which is often the best answer to “why didn’t they just…?”

For example, SE-0296 async/await, SE-0306 Actors, SE-0335 Introduce existential any, SE-0380 if and switch expressions, and SE-0382 Expression Macros are worth reading alongside the features themselves.

Trying features early

Many features can be tried before they’re final:

  • Upcoming feature flags enable source-breaking changes ahead of a new language mode, one at a time:
// In Package.swift:
// .target(
//     name: "App",
//     swiftSettings: [
//         .enableUpcomingFeature("ExistentialAny"),
//     ]
// )
  • Experimental features (.enableExperimentalFeature("…")) gate work-in-progress implementations. Don’t ship code that depends on them.
  • Toolchain snapshots from swift.org include the latest compiler from main.

Language modes and source compatibility

Swift takes source compatibility seriously. Most changes are additive, and existing code keeps compiling. Source-breaking changes are grouped into language modes: Swift 6 mode, for example, turns on full data-race safety checking. A newer compiler still supports older modes, so each module can migrate when it’s ready, even within the same project.

// swiftSettings: [.swiftLanguageMode(.v5)]   // keep a target on Swift 5 mode for now

You can check the compiler and language mode in code:

#if swift(>=6.0)
let languageModeNote = "Compiled in Swift 6 language mode or later"
#else
let languageModeNote = "Compiled in an older language mode"
#endif

#if compiler(>=6.0)
let compilerNote = "Built with a Swift 6 or newer compiler"
#endif

Who decides?

Swift is an open-source project with a published governance structure. The Core Team oversees the project as a whole, and steering groups and workgroups own specific areas: the Language Steering Group for the language and standard library, plus groups for areas like the ecosystem, platforms, and documentation. Many members work at Apple, but the process is public, and proposals regularly come from the community.

How to take part

  • Read and follow proposals in areas you care about, and try them on real code.
  • Give feedback during reviews, especially concrete experience: “I tried this in my codebase, and here’s what happened” is the most valuable kind.
  • Pitch when you have a well-understood problem; start with the problem, not the syntax.
  • Contribute to the compiler, standard library, or documentation. The Swift repositories label good first issues.

Summary

  • Swift Evolution is the public process every language change goes through: pitch, proposal, implementation, review, decision.
  • Proposals live on GitHub as numbered SE documents and are discussed on the Swift Forums.
  • Upcoming feature flags and toolchain snapshots let you try changes early; language modes group source-breaking changes.
  • Anyone can read, review, and contribute.

entry.title: Swift Package Manager: A Practical Guide

link.title: Swift Package Manager: A Practical Guide

entry.content:
Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) is the official tool for building, sharing, and depending on Swift code. It’s built into the Swift toolchain and into Xcode, needs no extra installation, and has become the default way to add libraries to Apple-platform projects. It’s also a great way to split your own app into modules.

Packages, products, and targets

  • A package is a folder with a Package.swift manifest and source code.
  • A target is a unit of code, a module: Sources/MyLibrary/… becomes the MyLibrary module. Test targets live in Tests/.
  • A product is what the package offers to others: a library (one or more targets) or an executable.

Creating a package

From the terminal:

mkdir Greeting && cd Greeting
swift package init --type library
swift build
swift test

Or in Xcode: File → New → Package. The result:

Greeting/
├── Package.swift
├── Sources/
│   └── Greeting/
│       └── Greeting.swift
└── Tests/
    └── GreetingTests/
        └── GreetingTests.swift

The manifest

Package.swift is written in Swift, using the PackageDescription API:

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "Greeting",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v16), .macOS(.v13)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "Greeting", targets: ["Greeting"]),
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(url: "https://github.com/apple/swift-collections.git", from: "1.1.0"),
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "Greeting",
            dependencies: [
                .product(name: "Collections", package: "swift-collections"),
            ]
        ),
        .testTarget(
            name: "GreetingTests",
            dependencies: ["Greeting"]
        ),
    ]
)

The first-line comment, swift-tools-version, is required. It sets the minimum SwiftPM version and the manifest API available, and with 6.0 and later, the default Swift language mode.

Versions and resolution

SwiftPM follows semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Common requirements:

Requirement Accepts
from: "1.1.0" 1.1.0 up to, but not including, 2.0.0 (the usual choice)
.upToNextMinor(from: "1.1.0") 1.1.x only
exact: "1.1.3" exactly that version (avoid in libraries)
branch: "main" / revision: "…" a branch or commit (for development only)

Resolved versions are recorded in Package.resolved. Commit it for apps so everyone builds the same versions; libraries usually don’t commit it. swift package update (or File → Packages → Update to Latest Package Versions) moves to the newest allowed versions.

Adding packages to an app

In Xcode: File → Add Package Dependencies…, paste the repository URL, pick a version rule, and choose which products to link to which targets. Xcode manages the dependency in the project file rather than a Package.swift.

Resources

Targets can include files like images, JSON, and localized strings:

// .target(
//     name: "Greeting",
//     resources: [.process("Resources")]    // optimized, e.g. asset catalogs compiled
// )

Access them through the generated Bundle.module:

// let url = Bundle.module.url(forResource: "greetings", withExtension: "json")

.process lets SwiftPM optimize files for the platform; .copy keeps a folder structure exactly as is.

Modularizing your own app

Packages aren’t just for third-party code. Splitting an app into local packages, like Networking, DesignSystem, and FeatureProfile, brings real benefits:

  • Faster builds, since unchanged modules aren’t recompiled.
  • Clear boundaries, because access control enforces what each module exposes.
  • Fast tests for each module, without launching the whole app.
  • SwiftUI previews that build only the module you’re working on.

Drag a local package folder into your Xcode project, then link its products to the app target.

Binary targets and plugins

  • Binary targets distribute closed-source XCFrameworks: .binaryTarget(name:url:checksum:).
  • Build tool plugins generate code during the build, like SwiftGen or protocol buffers.
  • Command plugins add commands such as formatting: swift package plugin <name>.
  • Macros are distributed as packages too; see Macros in Swift.

Useful commands

swift build -c release         # build optimized
swift test --parallel          # run tests in parallel
swift run MyTool               # build and run an executable product
swift package resolve          # resolve dependencies
swift package show-dependencies

Summary

  • A package has a Package.swift manifest, targets (modules), and products (what others can use).
  • Dependencies use semantic versioning; commit Package.resolved for apps.
  • Targets can bundle resources, accessed through Bundle.module.
  • Local packages are a great way to modularize an app; plugins, binary targets, and macros extend SwiftPM further.
entry.summary: Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) is the official tool for building, sharing, and depending on Swift code. It’s built into the Swift toolchain and into Xcode, needs no extra installation, and has become the default way to add libraries to Apple-platform projects. It’s also a great way to split your own app into modules.

entry.title: Operation and OperationQueue in Swift
entry.content:
Before async/await, there were two main ways to run work concurrently on Apple platforms: Grand Central Dispatch for lightweight blocks, and Operation with OperationQueue for work that needed dependencies, cancellation, priorities, and limits on concurrency. Operations are built on top of GCD, they’re still common in large codebases, and some of their ideas are worth knowing even if you write new code with Swift concurrency.

The basics

An OperationQueue runs Operation objects, using as many threads as it decides are useful. The simplest operation is a block:

import Foundation

let queue = OperationQueue()
queue.name = "com.example.images"
queue.maxConcurrentOperationCount = 2     // at most two at a time

queue.addOperation {
    print("Resizing image 1")
}

let compress = BlockOperation {
    print("Compressing")
}
queue.addOperation(compress)

maxConcurrentOperationCount = 1 turns the queue into a serial queue.

Dependencies

Dependencies are where operations shine. An operation doesn’t start until all of its dependencies have finished, even if they’re on different queues:

let download = BlockOperation { print("1. Download") }
let decode = BlockOperation { print("2. Decode") }
let save = BlockOperation { print("3. Save") }

decode.addDependency(download)
save.addDependency(decode)

let workQueue = OperationQueue()
workQueue.addOperations([save, decode, download], waitUntilFinished: true)
// Always prints 1, 2, 3, whatever order they were added in.

Be careful not to create cycles: two operations depending on each other will never run.

Cancellation

Calling cancel() on an operation, or cancelAllOperations() on a queue, marks operations as cancelled. Operations that haven’t started yet won’t run their main work. Running operations must check isCancelled themselves; cancellation is cooperative:

final class ThumbnailOperation: Operation, @unchecked Sendable {
    let imageIDs: [Int]
    private(set) var processed = 0

    init(imageIDs: [Int]) {
        self.imageIDs = imageIDs
    }

    override func main() {
        for _ in imageIDs {
            if isCancelled { return }      // stop promptly when cancelled
            processed += 1
        }
    }
}

let thumbnails = ThumbnailOperation(imageIDs: Array(1...100))
let thumbnailQueue = OperationQueue()
thumbnailQueue.addOperation(thumbnails)
thumbnails.cancel()

Subclassing Operation and overriding main() is the standard way to write reusable, testable units of work. @unchecked Sendable acknowledges that Operation subclasses manage their own thread safety, which Swift 6’s checker can’t verify.

Priorities and quality of service

let urgent = BlockOperation { print("User is waiting for this") }
urgent.queuePriority = .high
urgent.qualityOfService = .userInitiated

let background = OperationQueue()
background.qualityOfService = .utility

queuePriority orders ready operations within a queue. qualityOfService tells the system how important the work is for CPU and energy scheduling.

Waiting and completion

let report = BlockOperation { print("Building report") }
report.completionBlock = {
    print("Report finished")        // runs on a background thread
}

let reportQueue = OperationQueue()
reportQueue.addOperations([report], waitUntilFinished: true)

completionBlock runs on an arbitrary thread, so hop to the main queue before touching UI. And never call waitUntilFinished: true on the main thread: it blocks the UI.

Observing the queue

Operation properties like isExecuting, isFinished, and isCancelled are KVO-compliant, and so is OperationQueue.operationCount. That’s how progress UIs and asynchronous operations traditionally worked; see Key-Value Observing in Swift.

Asynchronous operations, which wrap callback-based work like a network request, must manage those KVO notifications themselves by overriding isAsynchronous, isExecuting, and isFinished. It’s notoriously easy to get wrong, and it’s one of the main reasons people moved to Swift concurrency.

Operations vs. GCD vs. Swift concurrency

Need Good fit
Fire off a quick block in the background GCD or a Task
Complex dependency graphs between units of work OperationQueue
Limiting concurrency, e.g. at most 3 downloads OperationQueue, or a task group with a counter
Structured cancellation and readable async code Swift concurrency
Protecting shared mutable state actors

In new code, Swift concurrency covers most of what operations offered, with less ceremony: task groups for parallel work, cooperative cancellation built in, and async let for simple dependencies. Operations remain a solid choice when you have a real dependency graph, or when you’re working in an existing codebase built around them. See Swift Concurrency for the modern approach.

Summary

  • OperationQueue runs Operations concurrently, with optional limits on how many run at once.
  • Dependencies order work across queues; cancellation is cooperative through isCancelled.
  • Subclass Operation and override main() for reusable units of work.
  • Operations are built on GCD; for new code, Swift concurrency is usually simpler.

entry.title: Swift Concurrency: async/await, Tasks, and Actors

link.title: Swift Concurrency: async/await, Tasks, and Actors

entry.content:
For years, asynchronous Swift code meant completion handlers, nested closures, and manual thread hopping. Swift concurrency replaces that with three ideas built into the language: async/await for writing asynchronous code that reads top to bottom, tasks for running work concurrently, and actors for protecting shared state from data races, checked by the compiler.

async and await

A function marked async can suspend while it waits for something, without blocking a thread. Callers mark each potential suspension point with await:

struct Profile {
    let name: String
}

func fetchProfile(id: Int) async throws -> Profile {
    try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(100))     // stand-in for a network call
    return Profile(name: "User \(id)")
}

func showProfile() async {
    do {
        let profile = try await fetchProfile(id: 42)
        print(profile.name)
    } catch {
        print("Failed: \(error)")
    }
}

Compare that with the completion-handler version: no nested closures, normal do/catch error handling, and no way to forget to call the completion handler on some path.

Suspending is not blocking. While fetchProfile waits, the thread is free to run other work. When the result is ready, the function resumes, possibly on a different thread.

Calling async code from sync code: Task

You can only await inside an async context. To start async work from synchronous code, like a button action, create a Task:

func buttonTapped() {
    Task {
        await showProfile()
    }
}

A task is a unit of asynchronous work. It inherits the actor it’s created on, so a task started from main-actor UI code also runs on the main actor, which is usually what you want for updating the UI.

Running work in parallel

await one call after another and they run sequentially. To run independent work at the same time, use async let:

func loadDashboard() async throws -> (Profile, Profile) {
    async let first = fetchProfile(id: 1)       // starts immediately
    async let second = fetchProfile(id: 2)      // also starts immediately
    return try await (first, second)            // wait for both
}

For a dynamic number of child tasks, use a task group:

func fetchAll(ids: [Int]) async throws -> [Profile] {
    try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: Profile.self) { group in
        for id in ids {
            group.addTask { try await fetchProfile(id: id) }
        }
        var profiles: [Profile] = []
        for try await profile in group {
            profiles.append(profile)
        }
        return profiles
    }
}

This is structured concurrency: child tasks can’t outlive their scope. If one child throws, or the parent is cancelled, the remaining children are cancelled automatically.

Cancellation

Cancellation in Swift is cooperative: cancelling a task sets a flag, and the task decides when to stop. Many system APIs, like Task.sleep and URLSession, check it for you. In your own loops, check it yourself:

func processLargeFile(lines: [String]) async throws -> Int {
    var count = 0
    for line in lines {
        try Task.checkCancellation()     // throws CancellationError if cancelled
        count += line.count
    }
    return count
}

let job = Task {
    try await processLargeFile(lines: ["a", "b"])
}
job.cancel()

Actors: safe shared state

A data race happens when two threads access the same memory at the same time and at least one writes. Actors prevent them: an actor’s mutable state can only be accessed by one task at a time.

actor BankAccount {
    private(set) var balance = 0

    func deposit(_ amount: Int) {
        balance += amount
    }

    func withdraw(_ amount: Int) -> Bool {
        guard balance >= amount else { return false }
        balance -= amount
        return true
    }
}

func useAccount() async {
    let account = BankAccount()
    await account.deposit(100)          // `await`: we may have to wait our turn
    let ok = await account.withdraw(30)
    print(ok, await account.balance)
}

From outside, every access to an actor is awaited, because the actor might be busy. Inside, code runs one call at a time, so no locks are needed.

Reentrancy

While an actor method is suspended at an await, other calls can run on the actor. Don’t assume state is unchanged after an await inside an actor method: check it again.

The main actor

UI code must run on the main thread. @MainActor expresses that in the type system:

@MainActor
final class ProfileViewModel {
    var title = "Loading…"

    func load() async {
        do {
            let profile = try await fetchProfile(id: 7)   // runs off the main actor
            title = profile.name                          // back on the main actor
        } catch {
            title = "Error"
        }
    }
}

The compiler ensures title is only touched on the main actor. No more DispatchQueue.main.async.

Sendable and data-race safety

Values passed between concurrency domains, like into a task or an actor, must be safe to share. That’s what the Sendable protocol marks: value types made of sendable parts, actors, and immutable or internally synchronized classes. In Swift 6 language mode, the compiler checks all of this and reports potential data races as errors at compile time. Migrating an existing project can take work, but the payoff is a whole class of bugs that can’t reach production.

Bridging old callback APIs

Wrap completion-handler APIs with a continuation:

func legacyFetch(completion: @escaping @Sendable (Result<String, Error>) -> Void) {
    completion(.success("data"))
}

func modernFetch() async throws -> String {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        legacyFetch { result in
            continuation.resume(with: result)    // must be resumed exactly once
        }
    }
}

Summary

  • async functions can suspend without blocking threads; await marks every suspension point.
  • Task starts async work from sync code; async let and task groups run work in parallel with structured cancellation.
  • Cancellation is cooperative: check Task.checkCancellation() in long loops.
  • Actors and @MainActor protect state; Sendable and Swift 6 mode turn data races into compile errors.

Swift concurrency replaces that with three ideas built into the language: async/await for writing asynchronous code that reads top to bottom, tasks for running work concurrently, and actors for protecting shared state from data races, checked by the compiler.

entry.title: Macros in Swift
entry.content:
Swift macros, introduced in Swift 5.9, generate code at compile time. Write @Observable on a class or #Preview in a SwiftUI file, and the compiler expands it into ordinary Swift code that you can inspect, step through, and reason about. Unlike C macros, Swift macros are type-checked, structured, and can’t silently change the meaning of code around them.

Using macros

You’ve probably used macros already. There are two kinds.

Freestanding macros start with # and appear on their own, like an expression or a declaration:

import SwiftUI

#Preview {
    Text("Hello, macros")
}

#Preview generates the type that registers a preview with Xcode. Other examples: #expect(...) in Swift Testing, and #warning("...").

Attached macros start with @ and are attached to a declaration, adding to it or generating code alongside it:

import Observation

@Observable
final class Counter {
    var count = 0
}

@Observable adds observation tracking: every stored property gets accessors that report reads and writes, and the class gains conformance to the Observable protocol. SwiftUI uses that to redraw only the views that actually read a changed property.

Seeing what a macro generates

Nothing about a macro is hidden. In Xcode, right-click a macro and choose Expand Macro to see the generated code inline. That’s a big difference from C macros or runtime magic: you can read exactly what you’re running, set breakpoints in it, and see errors pointing at the expanded code.

The kinds of macros

Role Spelled What it can do
Expression #name(...) Produce a value, e.g. #URL("https://…")
Declaration #name(...) Produce new declarations
Peer @Name Add declarations next to the one it’s attached to
Accessor @Name Add get/set accessors to a property
Member @Name Add members to a type
Member attribute @Name Add attributes to a type’s members
Extension @Name Add an extension, e.g. a protocol conformance

@Observable combines several roles: member, member attribute, and extension.

How macros are built

A macro has two parts:

  1. A declaration, in your library, that says what the macro looks like and where its implementation lives.
  2. An implementation, in a separate compiler plugin, that receives the source code as a syntax tree and returns new syntax. Implementations use Apple’s SwiftSyntax package.

Here’s the classic example from Xcode’s macro template: #stringify(x + y) returns both the value and the source text.

The declaration:

@freestanding(expression)
public macro stringify<T>(_ value: T) -> (T, String) =
    #externalMacro(module: "MyMacrosPlugin", type: "StringifyMacro")

The implementation, which runs inside the compiler:

import SwiftCompilerPlugin
import SwiftSyntax
import SwiftSyntaxMacros

public struct StringifyMacro: ExpressionMacro {
    public static func expansion(
        of node: some FreestandingMacroExpansionSyntax,
        in context: some MacroExpansionContext
    ) -> ExprSyntax {
        guard let argument = node.arguments.first?.expression else {
            fatalError("compiler bug: the macro does not have any arguments")
        }
        return "(\(argument), \(literal: argument.description))"
    }
}

@main
struct MyMacrosPlugin: CompilerPlugin {
    let providingMacros: [Macro.Type] = [StringifyMacro.self]
}

And at the call site:

// let (result, code) = #stringify(17 + 25)
// result == 42, code == "17 + 25"

The easiest way to start is File → New → Package → Swift Macro in Xcode, which sets up the declaration, plugin, and test targets for you.

Validating input and reporting errors

Because a macro sees real syntax, it can check its input and emit compiler diagnostics. A #URL("…") macro, for example, can verify the string at compile time and return a non-optional URL, turning a runtime crash into a compile error with a clear message. That’s a capability no function can offer.

Testing macros

SwiftSyntax includes assertMacroExpansion, which compares a macro’s input with the exact source it expands to. Macro tests run like any other unit tests, and they’re essential: a macro bug becomes a bug in every place the macro is used.

Macros vs. other tools

Need Best tool
Reusable get/set logic for one property Property wrapper
Shared behavior across types Protocol with an extension
Generating boilerplate that needs to see a whole type Macro
Checking a literal at compile time Expression macro

Reach for macros when other abstractions can’t express what you need. They add a compiler plugin to your build, and they’re harder to write than a function.

Costs to keep in mind

  • Build time: macro packages depend on SwiftSyntax, which is large and can noticeably slow down clean builds.
  • Trust: a macro plugin runs code during your build. Xcode asks you to approve macros from packages for that reason.
  • Readability: a macro can generate a lot of code from one line. Keep their behavior obvious and well documented.

Summary

  • Macros generate Swift code at compile time; freestanding macros use #, attached macros use @.
  • Expanded code is visible in Xcode, debuggable, and type-checked.
  • Implementations live in compiler plugins built with SwiftSyntax, and can emit real compiler errors.
  • Use macros for boilerplate and compile-time checks that functions, protocols, and property wrappers can’t handle.
